ruststream-rumqttc is the MQTT 5 broker for RustStream, built on the rumqttc client. The guides take an MQTT service from installation to production. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how MQTT 5 works, where ruststream-rumqttc sits between the MQTT broker and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-rumqttc costs on every message: throughput against the raw rumqttc client, and instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs each scenario three ways on a real MQTT server. Raw client drives rumqttc directly. Broker crate drives this crate's subscription with a loop of its own and no runtime. RustStream is the service a user writes, a #[subscriber] handler in an app. The first gap is what this crate costs over the client it wraps, and the second is what the runtime adds on top. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw client's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw client is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. The two scenarios are the two qualities of service a service reads at. At QoS 0 the server sends each message and settles nothing. At QoS 1 the service acknowledges each delivery with a PUBACK, as Path draws.

The second chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state. Each scenario is a service on MqttBroker reading a QoS 1 topic on the same server. The service runs on one thread, and the task that polls the rumqttc event loop runs there too, so the count holds the framework, this crate and the client's own work on the socket, the PUBACK included. The producer's thread is not counted. Cold start is what connecting, subscribing and taking the first message cost once.

How ruststream-rumqttc measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real MQTT server, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on MQTT.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. rumqttc driven directly: its event loop polled on a task of its own, which hands each delivery to the consumer over a channel, as this crate does. The consumer decodes it and, at QoS 1, acknowledges it. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, the descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the connection options (manual acknowledgements, a Receive Maximum of 1000, a 1 MiB packet ceiling), the quality of service of the subscription and of the publish, the place of the ack, the decode into the same struct, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. The body is 512 bytes of JSON. It decodes into a struct of two integer fields, so the decode allocates nothing and the number is about this crate rather than about the JSON parser.

A fresh topic and fresh client ids per run. A run never sees what an earlier one left. The consumer subscribes first. A publisher on a second connection then feeds it, and stays at most 768 messages ahead. At QoS 1 that keeps every delivery inside the Receive Maximum window of 1000; at QoS 0 it keeps the publisher from running away. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is decoded, before its acknowledgement leaves, in all three loops. Connecting and subscribing are outside it. The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate on 50000 messages, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. QoS 2 is not measured. Its four-packet handshake makes the server's bookkeeping the subject. A row is broker-bound when the consumer spent most of the run waiting on the server. That is arithmetic: a probe times 20000 QoS 1 publishes whose PUBACK it waits for, on a connection of its own, and takes the mean. The transport states how many round trips one delivery costs, and the row is flagged when their product reaches half the measured time per message. A QoS 0 delivery costs no round trip, because nothing travels back. A QoS 1 delivery costs one, the PUBACK. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, on MqttBroker against the same server, built without the testing feature, on a single-threaded runtime. A feeder on a thread of its own publishes the run's messages at QoS 1 before the measured region opens. The server holds them for the session, and the region drains them all. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 500, then 1000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. 500 is the most a run takes: twice that fills the Receive Maximum of 1000. The server is real, so a count moves a little between runs: how the socket hands the client its bytes depends on timing. A run fails when a scenario allocates more than the floor it declares, its cold start plus its steady cost per delivery. Against a saved baseline it also fails on two percent more instructions in a scenario.

just bench The recipe starts the stand from docker-compose.test.yml, runs both comparison scenarios, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes a few minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count takes about a minute and needs valgrind. It installs the benchmark runner at the release Cargo.lock pins. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it. A leading number counts over fewer deliveries (just bench-code 250); the published chart is counted at 500.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-rumqttc measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, on one server. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. The server runs on the same machine, in a container on the loopback. With no network latency, the same cost per message is a larger share of the time than it would be against a server across a network. Read the percentage as an upper bound on what a deployed service pays. A row reported as indistinguishable is one whose loops differ by less than the spread between their rounds. A figure below that noise would read as precision that was never measured, so none is published. A broker-bound row is one where the consumer waited on the server for most of the run. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside that wait, and the difference comes out near zero. That is a lower bound on the cost, not a measurement of it. A QoS 1 delivery costs one round trip and a QoS 0 delivery none, so the QoS 1 row is the one the mark can land on.

documents.t: An instruction count holds this crate's code, the runtime above it and the rumqttc work on the service's thread: the event loop's reads, the packet decode, the dispatch and the PUBACK. It moves a little between runs, because the server is real. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 500 deliveries and one of 1000. Connecting, subscribing and the first allocations behind them are the cold start, paid once.

A row is one subscription reading one topic, a small body and a single server. It measures what a delivery costs inside this crate, not what MQTT can carry. A share group, overlapping filters, a pool of worker lanes and QoS 2 each answer a different question, and the comparison measures none of them. The code chart counts a batch handler and a reply on the same stand. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, with no other benchmark on the machine, and the load average is recorded beside them. A loaded machine widens the spread between rounds, and a row inside that spread reads as indistinguishable.

Two handlers on the same filter, or the two members of a share group in one service, are one subscription on the server and two subscriptions in the service. The crate hands the filter's deliveries to them in turn. The filter stays subscribed while any of them is open, and a shutdown leaves it in the session. It is subscribed at the highest quality of service any of them asks for. Filters that differ but can match one topic, devices/+/telemetry next to devices/# or a share group next to a plain subscription on its filter, are separate subscriptions on the server. For a message that matches both, Mosquitto sends a packet for each. MQTT 5 lets a subscription carry an identifier, and the server names it in every packet it sends for that subscription. The crate gives an identifier only to a filter that overlaps another one on the connection, and routes each packet by the identifier it names. A filter that meets another one only after it was subscribed is subscribed again, with an identifier, and asks the server for no retained messages that time, so a retained message is not delivered twice. The identifier is derived from the filter itself. A restarted service that resumes a persistent session therefore gives each filter the identifier the server still holds. Subscription identifiers are optional for a server, and its CONNACK says whether it offers them. On a server that does not, opening a filter that overlaps another one on the same connection fails with an error naming both, before anything is subscribed. Two brokers with client ids of their own keep such filters apart. When a server sends one packet for two filters, the delivery to the first carries the acknowledgement, and the other's ack reports AckError::Unsupported. A packet no open subscription claims is held, because a resumed session sends its backlog before the service has opened the subscriptions it belongs to. Up to 1024 packets wait, and the oldest is dropped with a warning past that.

The lanes take the deliveries in turn, so deliveries of one topic run side by side on different lanes. Under workers(n, by_key) the partition-key header the publisher set picks the lane: the deliveries of one key run in order, and a delivery without the header takes the next lane in turn. Across processes, a share group divides the messages: the server hands each one to one member. The Receive Maximum bounds how many QoS 1 and QoS 2 deliveries a connection holds unacknowledged at once, across all its subscriptions. A batch handler takes up to the size the mount site names. A PUBLISH carries one message, so the crate assembles the batch on the client. A batch closes when it holds that size or 20 milliseconds after its first delivery.

Where ruststream-rumqttc sits: between the RustStream runtime and the rumqttc client, on one connection a task of its own drives. The runtime above it is the same for every broker. What is particular to MQTT is in this crate: the descriptors, what an ack sends, where a retry copy goes, the topic of a delivery and the mapping of headers onto MQTT 5 properties. Headers ride the protocol's own properties, so a peer written in any language reads a plain MQTT message. rumqttc splits a connection in two. The AsyncClient is a cloneable handle that queues requests: a subscribe, a publish, an acknowledgement. The EventLoop writes those requests to the socket and reads what the server sends, and it does both only while something polls it. Polling is also what sends the keep-alive pings and what moves acknowledgements. A connected broker holds one such pair. The crate polls the event loop on one task of its own, spawned at connect, which does nothing but poll and route. A slow handler therefore never stalls the connection: the pings, the acknowledgements and the other subscriptions' deliveries keep moving. Subscribing, publishing and acknowledging go through the AsyncClient from whichever task makes the call. The connection task hands each PUBLISH the server sends to the subscriptions it belongs to, one channel per subscription. Every subscription and publisher of the broker shares the one connection, so a service with many handlers holds one session on the server. Demultiplexing draws how one connection tells its subscriptions apart. How the pieces start and stop is on Lifecycle, and the way of one message on Path.

With the testing feature, TestApp::start connects the same broker to an in-process transport instead of a server. The descriptors, the policies and the deliveries are the production ones, and the transport reads the broker's own settings. A publish goes through the same validation and the same mapping of headers onto properties as on the wire. The transport models the server this connection talks to. It matches filters with + and # and keeps the $ rule. It sends one packet per matching subscription at the lesser quality of service, naming the subscription's identifier, and every packet goes through the same demultiplexing the connection task runs. So a share group takes one copy between its members, and overlapping filters each receive their own. It keeps the retained message of each topic, discards a message larger than max_packet_size, and refuses an acknowledgement after shutdown. What belongs to a server and a second connection runs only live: a persistent session and its redelivery on resume, the last will, the receive-maximum window, the QoS 1 and QoS 2 handshakes, access control, and several connections on one server. Each broker connected in process is a server of its own. Without the feature the transport is not compiled. A production build's connection handle is exactly the size of the AsyncClient it wraps, and the compiler checks that size.

It takes the URL, mqtt://host:port or mqtts://host:port, and the client id, and the builder's settings are recorded beside them. The runtime connects the broker when the app starts. Connect checks the settings first, before any I/O. A port that is not a number, a keep-alive under the client's 5-second minimum and TLS without a certificate authority to trust each fail the start with MqttError::Invalid, naming the setting. Then connect starts the connection task and waits up to 30 seconds for the server's first CONNACK. The task retries what the moment may cure, such as a server not up yet. A refusal the connection cannot outgrow ends the wait at once with MqttError::Connect: bad credentials, a client id the server rejects, a peer that does not speak MQTT, a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. A wait that runs out reports the last connection error it saw. Each subscription's descriptor resolves once, against the connected broker. It sends a SUBSCRIBE and waits for the SUBACK, so the server holds the subscription before the app reports that it started. A filter the server refuses fails the start with MqttError::Subscribe. While the service runs, the task reconnects a lost connection. It waits 100 milliseconds before the first attempt and doubles the wait up to 5 seconds. When the CONNACK reports the session gone, it subscribes every filter again. A refusal the connection cannot outgrow ends the task instead, and every subscription returns it as MqttError::Receive. Shutdown marks the connection closed first, so a publisher that aliases it cannot slip a message in. It then queues a DISCONNECT behind every acknowledgement already queued, and waits up to 5 seconds for the task to write them all. The server sees a clean end of the connection and publishes no last will. Shutdown returns nothing more: the closed state carries no diagnostics. A publisher paired before the shutdown is a handle the shutdown cannot take back. It answers MqttError::NotConnected. A delivery acknowledged after the shutdown reports a broker error. The in-process transport follows the same ladder. Its connect checks the settings as connect does, so a configuration the server path refuses is refused in a test too.

A subscription names a topic filter, which may hold wildcards. + stands for exactly one level. # stands for the rest of the topic, its parent level included, and comes last. A publish always names a full topic: this crate refuses a publish to a topic with a wildcard before anything is sent. A topic that starts with $, such as the server's own $SYS/..., is never matched by a filter that starts with a wildcard. A service reads such topics only by naming their first level. The server sends a message to each subscription that matches it. When one connection holds two filters that both match, MQTT 5 lets the server send one packet per subscription, each naming that subscription's identifier. Mosquitto does so, and this crate tells the copies apart by that identifier, as Demultiplexing draws. A share group shares the work. The filter $share/workers/devices/+/telemetry subscribes to devices/+/telemetry in the group workers, and the server hands each message to one session of the group. A subscription outside the group still gets its own copy. A publish with the retain flag set stays on its topic. The server keeps the last retained message of each topic and sends it to every new subscription whose filter matches, except a share group. A retained publish with an empty payload clears the topic. What a server keeps is that retained message per topic and the unacknowledged messages of a persistent session, which Sessions draws. A message that arrives while nothing matches it, and is not retained, is gone. A message carries headers as MQTT 5 properties. A user property is a pair of UTF-8 strings, and the content type, the response topic and the correlation data are properties of their own. This crate maps headers onto them, as Headers shows. An MQTT string must not hold U+0000, and a server may close the connection on other control characters, so the crate refuses a header or a topic that carries one. The model is the protocol's own, from the MQTT 5.0 standard: topic names and filters in section 4.7, shared subscriptions in 4.8.2, retained messages in 3.3.1.3. How a delivery is acknowledged is on Quality of service.

MQTT acknowledges a delivery with one packet at QoS 1 and a four-packet handshake at QoS 2; this crate sends the acknowledgement when the handler is done. A delivery travels at the lesser of the two, so a QoS 0 publish reaches a QoS 1 subscription at QoS 0. The Qos of a descriptor sets the subscription's side, and the publish policy sets the message's. At QoS 0 the server sends the PUBLISH and forgets it. Nothing travels back, so a QoS 0 delivery has nothing to acknowledge: ack reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs it. At QoS 1 and QoS 2 the server keeps the message until the service answers. This crate connects with manual acknowledgements, so rumqttc hands each PUBLISH to the subscription and sends nothing on its own. The acknowledgement leaves when the delivery is acknowledged, after the handler returns: PUBACK at QoS 1, PUBREC at QoS 2. The PUBREL and PUBCOMP that finish QoS 2 are exchanged by rumqttc itself. MQTT has no negative acknowledgement. A QoS 1 or QoS 2 delivery the service never acknowledges stays with the server, which sends it again only when a persistent session resumes on a new connection, marked as a duplicate. Sessions draws that resumption, and Settlement what each outcome of a handler sends. The client announces a Receive Maximum when it connects: how many QoS 1 and QoS 2 deliveries it takes without acknowledging them. Once that many are outstanding, the server sends no more QoS 1 or QoS 2 messages on the connection until one is acknowledged. This crate announces 1000 by default, and receive_maximum changes it. The window is the bound on what a slow subscription has waiting for it. QoS 0 deliveries take no part in it. A publish from the service returns once rumqttc has taken the message onto its request channel, which holds 64 requests, not once the server has acknowledged it. Each QoS 1 and QoS 2 publish is kept until the server acknowledges it. After a reconnect that resumes the session, rumqttc sends them again the way the protocol says. After a reconnect that starts a new session, the connection task sends them again as new publishes. The server cannot tell a message it already received, so such a message may arrive twice, at QoS 2 too. The flows are the protocol's own, from sections 4.3 and 4.9 of the MQTT 5.0 standard.

MqttBroker::new takes it beside the URL, and a second connection with the same id takes the session over. Two settings of the CONNECT decide whether the session outlives the connection. clean_start(false) asks the server to resume the session the client id already has. session_expiry says how long the server keeps it after the connection ends, in whole seconds. Without them a connection starts a clean session, which ends with the connection. The CONNACK answers whether the server found the session. When it reports none, this crate subscribes every filter again. When the session is present, the subscriptions are still on the server, and the QoS 1 and QoS 2 messages that arrived while the service was away, or that it never acknowledged, come next. Those messages can arrive before the subscription they belong to has opened, so the crate holds up to 1024 of them until it does. The keep-alive is the longest silence the connection allows. When nothing else travels, the client sends a PINGREQ, and the server ends a connection that stays silent for one and a half times the interval. rumqttc asks for 60 seconds unless keep_alive names another, and its minimum is 5 seconds. The last will is a message the CONNECT leaves with the server. The server publishes it when the connection ends without a DISCONNECT: a crash, a lost network, a keep-alive that ran out. A shutdown sends the DISCONNECT, so a service that stops cleanly publishes no will. Two more settings of the CONNECT bound what the server sends. The Receive Maximum is drawn on Quality of service. The Maximum Packet Size is the largest packet the client accepts, and the server discards a message larger than that for this client instead of sending it. This crate announces 1 MiB by default, and max_packet_size changes it. The CONNACK also says whether the server offers subscription identifiers, which Demultiplexing relies on. The session is the protocol's own, from sections 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1 of the MQTT 5.0 standard. How this crate opens and closes it is on Lifecycle.

The parts of ruststream-rumqttc an MQTT service uses, one page per component: the broker (MqttBroker), its subscriptions, its publish policy and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on. The broker pages cover its connection, session, last will, limits, startup and shutdown. The subscriptions read a topic or a filter with wildcards, with its quality of service and share group, overlapping filters and batches. Settlement is what each handler outcome sends on MQTT, with retries, the attempt cap and dead-letter topics. The context carries the topic a delivery was published to. Publishing covers the publish policy, the quality of service and retain flag of one message, headers and responders. The AsyncAPI pages show the mqtt bindings of the generated document. Testing runs the production app on an in-process MQTT server, and the same test against a running one.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks MQTT 5: the session the client opens, the QoS of each operation and the properties of each message. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's mqtt binding, version 0.2.0, to the parts it knows about. A server reports where the client connects, the protocol version 5 and the session it opens. An operation reports the quality of service it runs at. A message reports the MQTT 5 properties it rides. A reply named per request reports where its address is read. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors, the publish policies and the transforms. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-rumqttc = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label mqtt, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example mqtt_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Each message reports the MQTT 5 properties it rides: a delivery the response topic and correlation data, a published message the correlation data. The crate carries two headers in the protocol's own properties: correlation-id in Correlation Data and reply-to in Response Topic. The message binding describes them, each as a string. A message a subscription reads reports both. A requester sets the response topic on its own request, and a message a service publishes is not that request. So a message an Out slot or a reply sends reports the correlation data alone. Where a reply goes is the operation's reply object, and a reply named per request reports its address there. The payload format indicator stays out of the binding. It follows the media type one message carries in its content-type header, which no declaration knows. The document reports the media type of the position's codec in the contentType the core fills.

Telemetry reports correlationData and responseTopic; Alert, which the slot publishes, reports correlationData only. A receive operation reports the QoS its subscription reads at; a send operation reports the QoS and retain flag of its policy. The operation binding carries qos, the level as a number: 0, 1 or 2. A receive operation takes it from the descriptor's qos. A share group is part of the subscribed filter and adds nothing to the binding. A send operation comes from an Out slot or a dead-letter topic. It reports both arguments of the PUBLISH packet its publish policy declares: qos and retain. A reply has no send operation of its own, so a reply policy adds nothing to the document's operations.

The operation receive_devices___telemetry reports { "qos": 2 }. The slot's operation send_devices___telemetry_alerts_overheat reports { "qos": 1, "retain": true }, from the policy Publish::default().retain(true) the app attaches. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// Reads the fleet at `QoS` 2 as a member of `workers`, and raises an alert through its slot. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce).shared("workers"))] async fn collect( telemetry: &Telemetry, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher, Alerts>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature > 30.0 { let alert = Alert { device: telemetry.device.clone(), }; if let Err(err) = alerts.message(&alert).publish().await { tracing::warn!(subscription = "devices/+/telemetry", error = %err, "alert not published"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The fleet, read at `QoS` 2 as a member of `workers`. fn fleet() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry") .qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) .shared("workers") }

A reply named per request has no fixed channel, so the document points its address at the reply-to header of the request. A responder answers on the response topic its request carries. The crate maps that property onto the reply-to header, and a publish transform with Destination = Names reads it there. The document is built before any request arrives, so it cannot name the topic. The operation's reply.address.location is $message.header#/reply-to instead: a client reads the address of its answer from the header of its own request. The mount-site name, reply("devices/dev42/pong"), is the reply channel the document reports, and where a request without a response topic is answered. A reply that the type or the mount site names reports that channel alone.

The operation receive_devices_dev42_ping reports "location": "$message.header#/reply-to" in its reply address. The server reports host and port with MQTT 5 and the session binding: client id, clean start, keep-alive, expiry, last will, never credentials. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the broker's URL. A URL without a port reports the protocol's default: 1883 for mqtt://, 8883 for mqtts://. The protocol is mqtt and the protocolVersion is 5, the only version the crate speaks. The server binding describes the session the client opens. clientId is the client id of MqttBroker::new, and maximumPacketSize is the packet limit, 1 MiB by default. cleanSession, keepAlive and sessionExpiryInterval appear when the broker sets clean_start, keep_alive and session_expiry. lastWill reports the last will's topic, quality of service and retain flag. The will's payload is the content of a message, so it stays out. The user name and password of credentials stay out too.

The broker logs in, keeps its session for an hour and leaves a last will. Its server in the document is mqtt.internal:1883, with the session below and no password. { "bindingVersion": "0.2.0", "clientId": "telemetry-svc", "cleanSession": false, "keepAlive": 30, "sessionExpiryInterval": 3600, "maximumPacketSize": 1048576, "lastWill": { "topic": "devices/svc/status", "qos": 1, "retain": true } } Macros Manual examples/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The production server, with a persistent session and a last will. fn broker(password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new("mqtt://mqtt.internal:1883", "telemetry-svc") .credentials("telemetry-svc", password) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .last_will( "devices/svc/status", b"offline".to_vec(), Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_asyncapi.rs /// The production server, with a persistent session and a last will. fn broker(password: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new("mqtt://mqtt.internal:1883", "telemetry-svc") .credentials("telemetry-svc", password) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) .last_will( "devices/svc/status", b"offline".to_vec(), Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) }

MqttBroker connects a service to an MQTT 5 server; new only records the URL and the client id, and the runtime connects it at startup. MqttBroker::new takes the server's URL, mqtt://host:port or mqtts://host:port, and the client id. A URL without a port takes 1883, or 8883 for mqtts://. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: credentials and TLS, the session, the last will, the limits and the keep-alive. Each page gives the default a setting has when the service leaves it unset. The client id is the session's identity on the server. A second connection under the same id takes the session over, and the server closes the first one. So two instances of one service connect under two ids, and share their work through a share group. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedMqttBroker. The crate runs one task per connection: it drives the client's event loop, hands each delivery to its subscription, and reconnects when the connection is lost. Every subscription and every publisher of the service shares that connection. At shutdown the runtime closes it with a clean DISCONNECT. #[subscriber("devices/dev42/telemetry")] reads one topic at QoS 1. A MqttFilter reads many topics through the + and # wildcards, and the other descriptors are on the Subscriptions pages. The crate speaks MQTT 5 only: headers ride its user properties, and share groups exist only there. The crate has two features, both off by default. testing adds the in-process mode a TestApp test connects, and asyncapi adds the MQTT bindings of the generated document. The codec is the service's choice: json, msgpack or cbor on ruststream itself.

The service reads the telemetry of every device in the share group workers. A filter names no topic a retry copy could go to, so the mount site names one. cargo run --example mqtt_service --features testing -- run starts it against a server on localhost:1883. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_service.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers"))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // A filter matches many topics and names none of them, so the mount site says where // a retry copy is published. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_service.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; struct Record; impl Handle<Telemetry> for Record { fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn telemetry() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let record = subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record).map_source(|_| telemetry()); // A filter matches many topics and names none of them, so the mount site says where // a retry copy is published. b.include(record.build()) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) }

MqttError is the one error type of the crate: the connect, a subscription, a delivery, a publish, a closed connection and an invalid setting. Each variant names the step that failed. The client's errors become text inside it, so the rumqttc types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the server refused the connection, the TLS handshake failed, or no CONNACK came within 30 seconds Subscribe the server rejected a filter, or the connection ended while a subscription opened Receive the connection ended for good: the server refused a reconnect for a reason no retry changes Publish the topic is not one a server takes (empty, with a wildcard or a control character), a header has no MQTT form, or the connection task is gone NotConnected a publisher was used, or a subscription opened, after the broker shut down Invalid a setting or a descriptor cannot work, such as a keep-alive under five seconds or a share group with a / A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

An alert goes to the topic of its device. A device id with a wildcard makes no topic, so the handler logs the refusal and drops the reading: a retry would fail the same way. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber("broker-errors/telemetry")] async fn check(telemetry: &Telemetry, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let alert = Alert { temperature: telemetry.temperature, }; let topic = format!("alerts/{}", telemetry.device); if let Err(err) = alerts.message(&alert).to(&topic).publish().await { // A device id with `+` or `#` makes no topic, and no retry changes that. tracing::warn!( subscription = "broker-errors/telemetry", device = telemetry.device, error = %err, "alert not published" ); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_errors.rs struct Check; impl<Entry> Handle<Telemetry, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Check where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return Ok(()); } let alert = Alert { temperature: telemetry.temperature, }; let topic = format!("alerts/{}", telemetry.device); if let Err(err) = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&alert) .to(&topic) .publish() .await { // A device id with `+` or `#` makes no topic, and no retry changes that. tracing::warn!( subscription = "broker-errors/telemetry", device = telemetry.device, error = %err, "alert not published" ); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } }

last_will names the message the server publishes when the connection ends without a clean disconnect, such as a service's offline status. The will travels in the CONNECT packet, and the server keeps it for as long as the connection lasts. It has a topic, a payload, a QoS and a retain flag, like any publish. The payload is bytes, written as the service's readers decode them; no codec runs on it. The server publishes the will when the connection ends any other way than by the client's DISCONNECT. That covers a process that dies, a network that drops, a connection silent past its keep-alive, and a second client that takes the client id over. A clean shutdown sends a DISCONNECT, and the server discards the will. A retained will stays on its topic, so a dashboard that subscribes later still reads that the service is gone. The server publishes the will, so a TestApp test in process runs the app without it. A live test shows it. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the will's topic, QoS and retain flag, not its payload.

Each instance announces its own death on services/<client id>/status, retained. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_last_will.rs /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `{"online":false}` /// on the service's status topic and keeps it there for every later subscriber. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( format!("services/{client_id}/status"), r#"{"online":false}"#, Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_last_will.rs /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `{"online":false}` /// on the service's status topic and keeps it there for every later subscriber. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( format!("services/{client_id}/status"), r#"{"online":false}"#, Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

max_packet_size caps what the server may send, 1 MiB by default; receive_maximum caps unacknowledged QoS 1 and 2 deliveries, 1000 by default. Both travel to the server in the CONNECT packet, and the server holds itself to them. Both take a non-zero type, NonZeroU32 and NonZeroU16, because a server refuses a session that announces a zero limit. A constant such as const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); is checked when the service compiles. A message larger than max_packet_size never reaches the service: the server drops it for this client and delivers it to everyone else. The rumqttc client alone would allow 10 KiB and close the connection on a larger packet, so the crate raises its default to 1 MiB. A service whose payloads are larger raises it to fit them. receive_maximum is MQTT's flow control. The server sends QoS 1 and 2 deliveries until that many wait for an acknowledgement, then holds the rest until one is settled. So it also bounds what queues up in front of a slow handler. A delivery left unacknowledged holds its place until the connection ends: HandlerOutcome::retry(), for one, acknowledges nothing. Once every place is held, the server delivers no QoS 1 or 2 message on the connection, to any subscription, until the connection ends. QoS 0 deliveries need no acknowledgement and are not bounded. A TestApp test in process drops a message over max_packet_size as the server does. The window lives on the server, so it is for a live test.

Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_limits.rs const LARGEST_PACKET: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(256 * 1024).unwrap(); const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); /// Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .max_packet_size(LARGEST_PACKET) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_limits.rs const LARGEST_PACKET: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(256 * 1024).unwrap(); const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(100).unwrap(); /// Firmware images reach 256 KiB, and at most 100 deliveries wait for an acknowledgement. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .max_packet_size(LARGEST_PACKET) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc")) }

One glob, ruststream_rumqttc::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, Qos, the policy as Publish and the context key. use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; is the one import a routes file on MQTT writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds MqttBroker, the descriptors MqttTopic and MqttFilter, their quality of service Qos, and the context type MqttContext with its key DeliveryTopic. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is MqttPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on that name; the prefixed MqttPublish at the crate root tells them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher>, and names no broker type. So a file of handlers imports ruststream::prelude::* alone. The one exception is a body that sets the QoS or the retain flag of one message: it needs MqttPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude. MqttError is named where it is handled, from the crate root.

The descriptor, its QoS, the context key and the policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn check( telemetry: &Telemetry, Ctx(topic): Ctx<DeliveryTopic>, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } if alerts.message(&Alert { topic }).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { b.include(check) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*; struct Check; impl<Entry> Handle<Telemetry, (), Outs<(Entry,)>, MqttContext> for Check where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if telemetry.temperature <= 30.0 { return Ok(()); } let alert = Alert { topic: ctx.context(DeliveryTopic).to_owned(), }; if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&alert) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn telemetry() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let check = subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Check).map_source(|_| telemetry()); b.include(check.build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce)) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry") .build(); }, ) }

The connection task reconnects with a backoff from 100 ms to 5 s and resubscribes; keep_alive sets how soon a dead connection is noticed. A connection that fails after startup is dialed again after 100 ms. Each failed attempt doubles the wait, up to 5 seconds, and a successful connect resets it. A service notices nothing but the gap: its handlers keep running, and its subscriptions stay open. When the server reports that it no longer has the session, the task subscribes every filter again. With a persistent session the server still has it, together with what arrived during the gap. A refusal the connection will not outgrow ends the task instead: bad credentials, an unacceptable client id, a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. Every subscription then returns that error, as MqttError::Receive. keep_alive is how long the connection may stay silent. When nothing else is sent for that long, the client pings the server. The server closes a connection it has heard nothing from for one and a half keep-alive intervals, and publishes its last will. The client notices a server that stopped answering the same way, and reconnects. The default is 60 seconds, and the client's minimum is 5: a shorter one fails startup, in a TestApp test as on a server.

A silent connection is noticed within about 15 seconds. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives while the service reconnects is kept for it. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// A connection silent for 15 seconds is probed, and one that stays silent is dropped and dialed /// again. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives meanwhile is kept. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(15)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_reconnect.rs /// A connection silent for 15 seconds is probed, and one that stays silent is dropped and dialed /// again. The session outlives the gap by an hour, so what arrives meanwhile is kept. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(15)) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(1)) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

The login in the URL or credentials sends a user name and a password; tls_ca trusts a certificate authority and selects TLS, and tls_client_auth adds a client certificate. The user name and the password travel in the CONNECT packet. A server that refuses them fails startup at once, naming the refusal. A URL such as mqtt://user:password@host:1884 logs in with the user name and the password it carries. They are percent-decoded, as a URL writes them, so p%40ss is the password p@ss. The URL logs in only when it carries both a non-empty user name and a password. credentials is the explicit choice and wins over a login in the URL. TLS takes PEM bytes, so the service reads its files itself and hands their contents over. tls_ca is the certificate authority that signed the server's certificate. The client verifies the server against it and against no other store. So a TLS connection needs it: an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails startup, naming the missing setting. tls_ca also selects TLS on an mqtt:// URL. tls_client_auth takes the service's own certificate and key, for a server that verifies each client by its certificate, as managed MQTT services commonly do. A server may ask for both: a client certificate on a TLS listener, and a user name and a password inside the session. The login and the handshake happen on the server, so a TestApp test runs the same app in process without them. The settings are still checked as at the connect: an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails TestApp::start too. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and the port, never the credentials.

The service logs in with its user name and the password the environment gives it. clean_start(false) with a session_expiry keeps the session on the server, so a service that loses its connection gets what arrived meanwhile. An MQTT session belongs to a client id and lives on the server. It holds the client's subscriptions and the QoS 1 and 2 messages the client has not acknowledged yet. By default every connect starts a clean session, and the server forgets it when the connection ends. clean_start(false) asks the server to resume the session the client id already has. session_expiry says how long the server keeps it after the connection ends. The duration counts in whole seconds, and anything longer than u32::MAX seconds keeps the session with no end. Without an expiry the server drops the session with the connection, whatever clean_start says. While the session lives, the server queues every QoS 1 and 2 message that matches its subscriptions. When the service connects again under the same id, the server sends what it queued, then what arrives next. This covers a lost connection, a reconnect, a process that dies and a clean shutdown. A clean shutdown leaves the app's subscriptions in the session, so a service that restarts receives what was published while it was stopped. A QoS 0 message is never queued. A delivery the handler left unacknowledged, such as one HandlerOutcome::retry() settled, comes back when the session resumes. The session lives on the server, so a TestApp test in process starts a fresh one every time. What a session keeps is for a live test.

The server keeps the service's session for a day. A reading published while the service is down reaches it when it comes back. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_broker_session.rs /// The server at `url` keeps this client's session for a day after the service disconnects. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(24)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) } examples/manual/mqtt_broker_session.rs /// The server at `url` keeps this client's session for a day after the service disconnects. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(24)) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc")) }

Shutdown sends a clean DISCONNECT and waits up to 5 s for what is queued to leave; a publisher used afterwards reports MqttError::NotConnected. The runtime stops reading first and lets the handlers in flight finish. How long they get is the app's shutdown_timeout, with no bound by default. Their publishes and acknowledgements join the client's queue as they settle. Each subscription leaves its filter on the server as it closes, so a persistent session keeps the app's subscriptions, and the server queues what arrives until the service returns. Then the broker sends a DISCONNECT behind everything already queued. It waits up to 5 seconds for the connection task to write the queue out, and logs a warning when they run out. The server discards the last will of a connection that ends this way. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it returns MqttError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection. An acknowledgement after the shutdown is refused too.

The handlers get ten seconds to finish, and their alerts leave before the broker disconnects. Startup waits up to 30 seconds for the server's CONNACK; a refusal the connection cannot outgrow fails it at once, naming the cause. The runtime connects the broker first. The settings are checked before anything is dialed: a keep-alive under five seconds, an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca or a port that is not a number fail startup with MqttError::Invalid. Then the connection task dials the server. A server that is down or busy is dialed again with a backoff, until it answers or the 30 seconds run out. A timeout fails startup with MqttError::Connect, and the error carries the last reason a dial failed. Some refusals give the same answer on every attempt: wrong credentials, a client id the server rejects, a peer that is not an MQTT server, and a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. Each fails startup at once with MqttError::Connect, naming the refusal. A server that refuses a client certificate after the handshake answers the way a broken connection does, so that refusal is retried and reported when the 30 seconds run out. Once connected, the runtime opens every subscription, each one waiting for the server's SUBACK. A filter the server rejects fails startup with MqttError::Subscribe. The after_startup hooks run last, so a hook publishes through a connection whose subscriptions are already open. A TestApp test in process checks the settings as the connect does, then opens the subscriptions and runs the hooks. The dial and the server's refusals are for a live test.

Ctx<DeliveryTopic> gives a handler the topic a message was published to, which differs from the filter that matched it. MqttContext is what a delivery carries besides its payload and headers. The subscription builds it once per delivery. It holds one field, the topic, under the key DeliveryTopic. Both are in the prelude. A handler binds the topic as a parameter with Ctx<DeliveryTopic>, which hands it over as a String. A body that takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext> reads it borrowed with ctx.context(DeliveryTopic), as the manual form does. On an MqttFilter the topic tells the messages of the filter apart: devices/dev42/telemetry and devices/dev43/telemetry both match devices/+/telemetry. The subscription's name, ctx.name(), is the filter, never the topic. The same key reads the topic in a publish transform on the reply or the retry position, through cx.context(DeliveryTopic); a transform on the retry position sends a copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on.

An alarm names no device; the topic it arrived on does. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_context.rs /// The alarm itself names no device: its topic does, at the level the filter's `+` matched. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/alarms"), reply)] async fn open_incident(alarm: &Alarm, Ctx(topic): Ctx<DeliveryTopic>) -> Incident { let device = topic.split('/').nth(1).unwrap_or_default().to_owned(); tracing::info!(%topic, alarm.code, "incident opened"); Incident { device, code: alarm.code, } } examples/manual/mqtt_context.rs /// The alarm itself names no device: its topic does, at the level the filter's `+` matched. struct OpenIncident; impl Handle<Alarm, Incident, (), MqttContext> for OpenIncident { fn handle( &self, alarm: &Alarm, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Incident, HandlerOutcome>> { let topic = ctx.context(DeliveryTopic); let device = topic.split('/').nth(1).unwrap_or_default().to_owned(); tracing::info!(%topic, alarm.code, "incident opened"); ready(Ok(Incident { device, code: alarm.code, })) } }

MqttPublish, Publish in the prelude, sets the QoS and the retain flag; a publish returns once the client session owns the message. A PUBLISH packet carries two arguments besides the topic: a quality of service and the retain flag. The policy declares both: qos defaults to Qos::AtLeastOnce, and retain to false. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. A scope's after_startup hook takes one too, for a message the service sends once it is connected. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into an MqttPublisher. A reply mounted without a policy sends through Publish::default(), to the topic its type declares. A publish returns once the client session owns the message, not once the server confirmed it. At QoS 1 and 2 the session sends the message again until the server acknowledges it, across reconnects. A topic with a + or # wildcard is refused with MqttError::Publish. One message changes the arguments with the qos and retain steps.

Headers travel as MQTT 5 user properties; content-type, reply-to and correlation-id take the protocol's own properties. A peer in any language reads them as plain MQTT, with no envelope around the payload. content-type becomes the content type property, reply-to the response topic a responder answers on, and correlation-id the correlation data, in both directions. A message with no headers is published with no properties at all. A textual content type (application/json, any text/ type, any +json type) sets the payload format indicator to 1, which tells a peer the body is UTF-8; any other sets it to 0. A property is an MQTT string, and a server may close the connection on one with a control character. So a header name or value that is not UTF-8, or carries a control character or a Unicode non-character, refuses the publish with MqttError::Publish. The codec of a position writes no header, so nothing sets the content type unless the service does. A publish transform sets it at the mount site, once for every message of one position: the replies, a slot or the retry copies.

Every reply of the position states that its body is JSON: Macros Manual examples/mqtt_publishing_headers.rs /// States the media type of every message the position sends. The header fills the content type /// property and sets the payload format indicator, so a peer reads the body as UTF-8 JSON. The qos and retain steps change one message's QoS or retain flag over the policy; a handler bounds its slot with MqttPublishOptions. MqttPublishSteps puts both steps on the publish builder, in any order. An argument the call does not name keeps what the policy declared at the mount site. The values reach the client as the protocol fields they are, so a subscriber receives a plain message with no extra property. A publish with no call site of its own, a reply or a retry copy, takes the policy whole. The steps are reached from a slot whose bound names the options type: Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Slot>. That bound and this crate's prelude are the one place a handler body names the broker. A test reads what the steps set with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(&MqttPublishOptions::default().retain(true)).

A responder answers on the response topic a request carries, through a reply transform that also copies the correlation data. An MQTT 5 request carries the topic its answer goes to in the response topic property, and the handler reads it as the reply-to header. Its correlation data arrives as the correlation-id header, and the requester matches the answer to its question by it. A PublishTransform on the reply position reads both from the request: cx.headers().reply_to() and cx.headers().correlation_id(). It names the answer's topic, so it declares type Destination = Names. The reply type declares no topic of its own, which is what leaves the naming to the transform. The topic the mount site names, reply("..") in the macro form, is the fallback: a request without a response topic is answered there. The generated document points the reply's address at the request's reply-to header, as Replies shows.

A shared subscription receives no retained messages. A scope's after_startup hook runs once the broker is connected, which is where a service announces its own status. A state is bytes on the wire rather than an encoded model, so its type carries its own bytes with #[derive(Serialized)], and no codec runs on them.

An ack sends PUBACK at QoS 1 and PUBREC at QoS 2; QoS 0 has no acknowledgement, and MQTT has no negative one. A message settles when the handler returns, and the delivery's own quality of service decides what that sends. A delivery arrives at the lower of the publisher's QoS and the subscription's, so a QoS 1 subscription still receives a QoS 0 publish at QoS 0. At QoS 1 and 2 the server keeps a delivery until it is acknowledged; the client finishes the QoS 2 handshake on its own. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement packet, so settling it reports AckError::Unsupported, which the runtime logs as a warning. drop acknowledges the delivery too, because an acknowledgement is the only final answer MQTT has; the server never sends the message again. retry asks for a negative acknowledgement, which MQTT does not have, so the delivery stays unacknowledged. retry_after is the outcome that retries within the session. In the manual form Ok acknowledges and Err(outcome) settles by the outcome. When the server sends one packet for two overlapping filters, the acknowledgement belongs to one delivery, and settling the other reports Unsupported.

dead_letter(topic) names the topic a delivery that reached its cap is published to; it lies outside every filter the service reads. It follows max_attempts(n) at the mount site. When the n-th delivery asks for a retry, the runtime acknowledges it and publishes it to the dead-letter topic instead. The message keeps its payload and its headers. RETRY_COUNT_HEADER on it says how many times it was delivered. The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and a subscription of this service or of another one reads it. A filter of the service that matches the dead-letter topic receives the spent message as a new delivery, so the topic stays outside every other filter the service reads.

A filter subscription names where its retry copies go, once with out_retry(..).to(..) or per delivery with a transform. An MqttTopic reads one topic, and its copies go there; a share group's copies go to the plain topic, not to $share/... An MqttFilter matches many topics and is a topic of its own only by accident, so the mount site names the destination. out_retry binds the Retry slot, the one the runtime publishes its copies through, to a publish policy. .to(topic) sends every copy to one topic; a topic the filter matches brings the copies back to the same handler. A publish transform that declares Names picks the topic per delivery instead, such as the topic the delivery arrived on. It reads that topic from the MqttContext of the delivery, which reaches the slot when the handler reads it: a Ctx<DeliveryTopic> parameter, or a manual body typed over MqttContext. Naming a topic and adding a naming transform are mutually exclusive, and writing both does not compile. A filter registration that names neither does not start, and the error names the subscription. The copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so a codec on the slot encodes nothing, while a transform still runs.

max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries one message gets, counted on the retry-count header, because MQTT counts no redeliveries. A redelivered PUBLISH packet carries a duplicate flag and no counter. So the runtime counts on RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, which travels on the copies retry_after publishes. The cap counts deliveries, the first one included: nonzero!(5u32) gives a message five. Under a cap every retry travels as such a copy, an immediate retry() too, so the count reaches the cap whichever outcome the handler returns. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter topic instead of coming back. A cap without a dead-letter topic rejects the delivery, which on MQTT acknowledges it and lets it go; a warning names the subscription. A filter subscription also names where its copies go, with out_retry.

retry_after(delay) acknowledges the delivery, waits, then publishes a copy of the message with its retry count in a header. MQTT holds no message back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It acknowledges the original, waits out the delay and publishes the payload and the headers as they arrived. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, raised by one on every copy, and the handler reads it like any other header. An MqttTopic subscription receives its copies on its own topic; an MqttFilter names where they go with out_retry. The copy waits in the service's memory, so a process that exits before the delay is over loses it. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement, and its copy is published all the same. A copy is an ordinary publish, so every subscription whose filter matches its topic receives it, in this service and in any other. A retried topic therefore lies outside every other filter the service reads, or another handler reads the copy too. max_attempts caps the deliveries of one message.

A reading the database timed out on is written again five seconds later. retry() leaves a delivery unacknowledged: it comes back when a persistent session resumes, never within the connection. The outcome asks the broker for a negative acknowledgement, and MQTT has none. The runtime logs the refusal and moves on, and nothing acknowledges the delivery later. At QoS 1 and 2 the server keeps the message in the client's session. It sends the message again when the service connects with the same client id and the session is still there: clean_start(false) and a session_expiry longer than the gap. With a clean start, or once the session expired, the message is gone; at QoS 0 it is gone at once. Until the connection ends, the delivery holds one slot of the receive_maximum window, 1000 by default. When the window is full of unacknowledged deliveries, the server sends no more QoS 1 or 2 messages on that connection. For a retry within the session, a handler returns retry_after. A registration with a cap turns retry() into an immediate copy of the message instead.

A topic in #[subscriber] subscribes to that one topic at QoS 1; a descriptor carries wildcards, the quality of service and a share group. #[subscriber("devices/dev42/telemetry")] subscribes to the topic devices/dev42/telemetry. The bare name is an MqttTopic with its defaults: Qos::AtLeastOnce and no share group. A name with a + or # wildcard is a filter, not a topic, so the service does not start, and the error names MqttFilter, the descriptor that takes it. Every other setting belongs to a descriptor: MqttTopic for one topic, MqttFilter for a filter with wildcards. Each descriptor carries its quality of service and its share group. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor joins the chain through map_source. The subscription is open once the server has acknowledged it, before the service takes its first message.

A slice handler reads batches the crate assembles on the client: a batch closes at the size the mount site names or 20 ms after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. An MQTT packet carries one message, so the crate collects deliveries into batches on the client. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or 20 milliseconds after its first delivery, whichever comes first. The size is the mount site's, and the 20 ms deadline is the crate's. A subscription with nothing to read waits for its first delivery as long as it takes. Nothing at the mount site says which side of the wire filled a batch, so a batch handler written for another broker mounts here unchanged. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch, and a Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. Each delivery is acknowledged on its own. A batch abandoned while it fills leaves its deliveries unacknowledged. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery.

workers(n, by_key) keeps deliveries that share the partition-key header on one lane, in order, while other keys run in parallel. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes over one subscription. The lane of a delivery is picked by a hash of its partition key, so deliveries with one key run one after another, in the order they arrived. Deliveries with different keys run at once on different lanes. A delivery without a key goes to the next lane in rotation and keeps no order with any other. MQTT has no partitions, so the key is the header PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, partition-key, which travels as an MQTT 5 user property. The protocol gives the property no meaning: it is a convention between the publisher, which sets it, and this crate, which reads it back. A service that publishes to a keyed subscription sets the header on each message, such as the tenant or the device the message belongs to. The lanes order work inside one connection. A share group spreads messages over instances and keeps no order by key between them. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

b.include(checkout) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_lanes.rs use ruststream_rumqttc::PARTITION_KEY_HEADER; use ruststream_rumqttc::prelude::*;
