ready(Ok(())) } } /// The checkout keys every order it places by its tenant. struct Checkout; impl<Entry> Handle<Purchase, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Checkout where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, purchase: &Purchase, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let order = Order { id: purchase.id, tenant: purchase.tenant.clone(), }; let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, purchase.tenant.clone()); let placed = outs.get(DefaultSlot).message(&order).with_headers(key); if placed.publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "orders-svc"), |b| { // Eight lanes: one tenant's orders never run at the same time, and different // tenants run side by side. b.include( subscriber("orders/placed", Place) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build(), ); b.include(subscriber("checkout/completed", Checkout).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); }, ) }

MqttFilter subscribes with the + and # wildcards; each delivery carries its own topic, and the mount site names where retry copies go. MqttFilter::new takes the topic filter. + matches exactly one level of a topic, and # matches every level that remains, so it may only come last. A filter that starts with a wildcard does not match a topic that starts with $, such as the server's own $SYS topics. qos sets the quality of service, and shared puts the subscription in a share group. The subscription's name is the filter. A handler reads the topic each message was published to through DeliveryTopic. A filter with # before its last level, or one with a control character, stops the service at startup. A filter is no topic a publisher can use, so the subscription has no topic of its own for a retry_after copy. The mount site names one with .out_retry(policy).to(topic), or names one per delivery with a transform. A registration that names neither does not start, and the error names the subscription and MqttFilter. A destination the filter matches brings the copy back to this subscription.

The readings of every device, read at QoS 1; a retry copy goes to devices/retry/telemetry. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Collects the readings of every device: `+` stands for the device's own level of the topic. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn collect(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading collected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // A filter is no topic to publish to, so the mount site names where a retry copy // goes: a topic the filter matches, so the copy comes back here. b.include(collect) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Collects the readings of every device: `+` stands for the device's own level of the topic. struct Collect; impl Handle<Telemetry> for Collect { fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading collected"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let fleet = MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce); // A filter is no topic to publish to, so the mount site names where a retry copy // goes: a topic the filter matches, so the copy comes back here. b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Collect) .build() .map_source(|_| fleet), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) }

MqttTopic subscribes to one topic with no wildcard, so a retry copy published to that topic comes back with nothing named at the mount site. MqttTopic::new takes the topic. qos sets the quality of service, AtLeastOnce by default. shared puts the subscription in a share group. The subscription's name is the topic: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the topic is the channel of the AsyncAPI document. A topic is also a name a publisher can use. So a retry_after copy is published to the subscription's own topic, and the mount site names no destination for it. The copy is an ordinary publish, so every subscription whose filter matches the topic receives it too. A share group does not change where the copy goes: it is published to the plain topic. An empty topic, a topic with a + or # wildcard, or one with a control character stops the service at startup, before anything is subscribed. A wildcard belongs to MqttFilter, and the error names it.

Commands for one valve, read at QoS 2; a command the valve refuses comes back five seconds later. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// Runs the commands sent to dev42; the valve refuses the first attempt while it settles, so the /// command comes back as a copy five seconds later. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn execute(command: &Command, ctx: &mut Context) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(command.id, "valve settling, trying again"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(SETTLE); } tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("valves", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "valves-svc"), |b| { // The topic is where a copy goes, so the mount site names nothing. b.include(execute); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_topic.rs /// Runs the commands sent to dev42; the valve refuses the first attempt while it settles, so the /// command comes back as a copy five seconds later. struct Execute; impl Handle<Command> for Execute { fn handle( &self, command: &Command, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(command.id, "valve settling, trying again"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(SETTLE))); } tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("valves", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "valves-svc"), |b| { let commands = MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce); // The topic is where a copy goes, so the mount site names nothing. b.include( subscriber("devices/dev42/commands", Execute) .build() .map_source(|_| commands), ); }, ) }

Overlapping filters on one connection each receive a message once, told apart by subscription identifiers; one filter mounted twice shares it. Two filters overlap when one topic can match both, such as devices/+/telemetry and devices/dev42/#. They are two subscriptions to the server, and each receives a message once. The server sends a packet per matching subscription, and the crate tells the packets apart by MQTT 5 subscription identifiers. The crate attaches an identifier only to a filter that meets another one on the same connection. A share group next to a plain subscription on the same filter overlaps the same way. The same filter mounted twice, or two members of one share group, is one subscription to the server. The crate hands its deliveries to the mounts in turn, and the filter stays subscribed while any of them is open. A shutdown leaves it in the session. A server announces whether it offers subscription identifiers when the connection opens. On a server without them, a filter that meets another one on the same connection does not open, and the error names both filters. Two brokers with client ids of their own keep such filters on separate connections.

The fleet's readings and everything dev42 sends: a reading of dev42 reaches both handlers, once each. Each retry topic matches its own filter only, so a retry copy returns to the subscription that asked for it. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_overlaps.rs /// Records the readings of the whole fleet. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry"))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Watches everything dev42 sends, its readings included. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/dev42/#"))] async fn watch(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, "dev42 watched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // Each retry topic matches its own filter and not the other one, so a copy comes // back to the subscription that asked for it alone. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); b.include(watch) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/dev42/retry"); }, ) } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_overlaps.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { // Each retry topic matches its own filter and not the other one, so a copy comes // back to the subscription that asked for it alone. b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record) .build() .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry")), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); b.include( subscriber("devices/dev42/#", Watch) .build() .map_source(|_| MqttFilter::new("devices/dev42/#")), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/dev42/retry"); }, ) }

Qos picks at most once, at least once or exactly once; a delivery arrives at the lower of the publisher's and the subscription's level. A subscription names its level with qos(..) on MqttTopic or MqttFilter. The default is Qos::AtLeastOnce. Level QoS What the protocol does AtMostOnce 0 sends the message once, with no acknowledgement; a message lost on the way is gone AtLeastOnce 1 resends until the receiver answers PUBACK; a message may arrive twice ExactlyOnce 2 a four-packet handshake, so the message arrives once The server sends each message at the lower of two levels: the one its publisher sent it at and the one the subscription asked for. So a QoS 2 subscription receives a QoS 0 publish at QoS 0. A delivery at QoS 1 or 2 is acknowledged when the handler settles it. A delivery at QoS 0 has no acknowledgement packet, so settling it reports AckError::Unsupported. The level a publish is sent at is a setting of the publish policy.

Telemetry read at most once, because the next reading replaces a lost one, and valve commands read exactly once. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// A device reports every few seconds, so a lost reading costs nothing: at most once. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce))] async fn sample(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading sampled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A valve command must run once and never twice: exactly once. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn execute(command: &Command) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(command.id, command.open, "command executed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_qos.rs /// A device reports every few seconds, so a lost reading costs nothing: at most once. fn readings() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce) } /// A valve command must run once and never twice: exactly once. fn commands() -> MqttTopic { MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/commands").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) }

shared(group) makes a share group: the server hands each message to one member, and retained messages reach none of them. A share group is how MQTT 5 spreads messages over competing consumers. MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") subscribes $share/workers/devices/+/telemetry. MqttTopic::shared does the same for one topic. Every instance of a service that subscribes with the same group and the same filter is a member, and the server sends each message to one member only. A subscription outside the group on the same filter still receives every message. The group belongs to the subscribed filter alone. The subscription's name, the delivery's topic and the destination of a retry copy stay the plain form. A retained message is not sent to a share group. An empty group name, or one with /, + or #, stops the service at startup. Two members of one group on one connection are one subscription to the server, and the crate hands their deliveries out in turn.

Each instance of the telemetry service joins workers, so the fleet's readings are spread over the instances. Macros Manual examples/mqtt_subscriptions_shared.rs /// Every instance of the service joins the group `workers`, so each reading is handled once. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers"))] async fn process(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(device = %telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading processed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/mqtt_subscriptions_shared.rs /// Every instance of the service joins the group `workers`, so each reading is handled once. fn fleet() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").shared("workers") }

TestApp::start runs the production app on an in-process MQTT server: wildcards, share groups, retained messages and QoS, with no broker. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<MqttBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process server has no settings of its own. It reads the broker's, and checks them as the connect does: a keep-alive under five seconds or an mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails TestApp::start. A publish goes through the same validation and the same mapping onto MQTT 5 properties as on the wire. It routes as a server routes. A publish reaches every subscription whose filter matches its topic, + and # included, and a filter starting with a wildcard skips the topics that start with $. A share group hands each message to one of its members. Two overlapping filters each receive their own copy, as a server sends them. A delivery arrives at the lower of the publish and the subscription QoS, and a QoS 0 delivery has nothing to acknowledge. A retained message reaches every later subscription outside a share group, and an empty retained payload clears it. A message over the broker's max_packet_size never arrives, and a publish or an acknowledgement after shutdown is refused. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only a server has is for a live test: the login and TLS, a persistent session, the last will, the receive window, a lost connection, and several connections on one server.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-rumqttc = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The test publishes a hot reading to one device's topic, and reads how the handler settled it and the alert it published. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running MQTT server, for what only a server has: sessions, the last will, flow control. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so startup waits for the server's CONNACK and each subscription for its SUBACK. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process server leaves out: the login and TLS, a persistent session, the last will, the receive window, a lost connection, and several connections sharing one server. A server is shared with whatever else runs against it. So each run connects under a client id of its own: a second connection under one id takes the session over. In the example, live::url returns the server's address from MQTT_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is a Mosquitto container in docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts, with a listener that asks for a password and one that speaks TLS.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at MQTT_TEST_URL. This guide chooses a quality of service per subscription, shows what each handler outcome sends to the server, and keeps the messages a service misses while it is down. The example is a billing service. Meters report their energy usage, and every report is money, so none may be lost. They also report their power draw for a live chart, where a lost sample is replaced by the next one.

MQTT has three levels of quality of service: Level Guarantee Packets Qos::AtMostOnce (0) at most once: a message may be lost PUBLISH Qos::AtLeastOnce (1) at least once: a message may come twice PUBLISH, PUBACK Qos::ExactlyOnce (2) exactly once between two parties PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP The subscription names the level it reads at, and the publisher names the level it sends at. A delivery arrives at the lower of the two. So a meter that publishes its usage at QoS 1 reaches a QoS 2 subscription at QoS 1.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Usage is money: the server hands it over in the four-packet handshake, and the service /// acknowledges it only once it is posted. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("meters/+/usage").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce))] async fn bill(usage: &Usage) -> HandlerOutcome { if usage.kwh < 0.0 { tracing::warn!(usage.meter, "negative usage dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if let Err(err) = post(usage).await { tracing::warn!(usage.meter, %err, "usage left for the next session"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(usage.meter, usage.kwh, "usage billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Usage is money: the server hands it over in the four-packet handshake, and the service /// acknowledges it only once it is posted. struct Bill; impl Handle<Usage> for Bill { async fn handle( &self, usage: &Usage, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if usage.kwh < 0.0 { tracing::warn!(usage.meter, "negative usage dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if let Err(err) = post(usage).await { tracing::warn!(usage.meter, %err, "usage left for the next session"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(usage.meter, usage.kwh, "usage billed"); Ok(()) } } fn usage_of_every_meter() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("meters/+/usage").qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) } The broker acknowledges a delivery when the handler returns, not when it arrives. Each outcome sends what the protocol has for it: ack sends PUBACK at QoS 1 and PUBREC at QoS 2; the client finishes the QoS 2 handshake itself. drop acknowledges too: MQTT has no negative acknowledgement, and acknowledging is its only way to be done with a message. retry sends nothing. The report stays unacknowledged, and the server sends it again only when the service's session resumes on a new connection. A QoS 0 delivery has no acknowledgement at all. Its outcome reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning. bill returns retry when the ledger does not answer. The report then waits for the next session: after a restart, the server hands it over again. Retries and dead letters shows how to try again within the same session.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Power samples feed a live chart: a lost one is replaced by the next, so they travel at /// `QoS` 0 and are written in batches. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("meters/+/power").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce))] async fn chart(samples: &[Sample]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = samples.len(), "samples charted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Power samples feed a live chart: a lost one is replaced by the next, so they travel at /// `QoS` 0 and are written in batches. struct Chart; impl Handle<[Sample]> for Chart { fn handle( &self, samples: &[Sample], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = samples.len(), "samples charted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn power_of_every_meter() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("meters/+/power").qos(Qos::AtMostOnce) } A handler over a slice is a batch handler. A PUBLISH packet carries one message, so the broker assembles the batches on the client. A batch closes when it holds the size the mount site names, or 20 milliseconds after its first sample. Acknowledgement stays per delivery.

/// The server keeps the session of this client id for a day after the service disconnects. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id) .clean_start(false) .session_expiry(Duration::from_hours(24)) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("meters/+/usage", Bill) .map_source(|_| usage_of_every_meter()) .build(), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("meters/retry/usage"); // At most 64 samples per call; a batch with fewer closes 20 ms after its first sample. b.include( subscriber("meters/+/power", Chart) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build() .map_source(|_| power_of_every_meter()), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("meters/retry/power"); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "billing")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A session is what the server keeps for one client id: its subscriptions and the QoS 1 and 2 messages it has not acknowledged. clean_start(false) resumes the session the server kept, instead of starting a new one. session_expiry is how long the server keeps it after the service disconnects, a day here. While the service is down, the server queues the QoS 1 and 2 messages that match its subscriptions. When the service connects again under the same client id, the server sends them first. The broker holds them until the subscription that owns them opens, so none is lost at startup. The client id is the session's name, so each process of the service needs its own; Connecting to production shows one per deployment. Mosquitto does not queue QoS 0 messages for an absent session by default. The samples published while the service is down are gone, which is what a live chart wants.

One subscription hands its deliveries to the handler one at a time, in the order they arrived. workers(n) runs n handlers at once and gives that order up. workers(n, by_key) keeps it per key: the deliveries of one key run one after another, and different keys run side by side. The key is the partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, which the meter sets on each report, such as its own id. A report without the header takes the next lane in turn.

receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) tells the server how many QoS 1 and 2 deliveries the service takes before it acknowledges one. At the limit the server stops sending until a handler settles a delivery. The default is 1000. An unacknowledged delivery holds its place in that window until the connection ends, so every retry without a declared cap takes one place away until the next session. QoS 0 deliveries have no such window: a handler slower than its publishers lets them queue in memory without a bound.

The in-process tests check what bill settles for each report and that three samples published at once arrive as one batch. A session, its resumption and the receive-maximum window live on a server, so one test runs against Mosquitto: MQTT_TEST_URL=mqtt://localhost:1883 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 It starts the service, ends its connection abruptly, publishes a usage report while the service is down, and starts the service again under the same client id. The report published while the service was down is the first one bill receives. Without MQTT_TEST_URL the test returns at once. Testing an MQTT service shows the pattern.

This guide keeps the current state of every device on the server, so a reader that starts later sees it at once, and announces whether the service itself is running. MQTT keeps no history, with one exception: a retained message. The server keeps the last retained message of each topic and sends it to every new subscription whose filter matches. The last will is a message the server publishes for a client whose connection ends without a clean disconnect. The example is a gateway monitor. Gateways send heartbeats with their battery level. The service keeps the state of each gateway, ok or low-battery, retained on gateways/<id>/state, and dashboards read it from there.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The state of one gateway, as plain text a dashboard shows as it is. The type carries its own /// bytes, so no codec runs on them, and the `{gateway}` level becomes a setter. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "gateways/{gateway}/state")] struct GatewayState(Vec<u8>); #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(GatewayState)] struct States; /// Turns each heartbeat into the gateway's state. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("gateways/+/heartbeat").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn track(heartbeat: &Heartbeat, Out(states): Out<impl Publisher, States>) -> HandlerOutcome { let state = if heartbeat.battery_percent < 20 { "low-battery" } else { "ok" }; let announced = states .message(&GatewayState(state.as_bytes().to_vec())) .to() .gateway(&heartbeat.gateway) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = announced { tracing::warn!(heartbeat.gateway, %err, "state not announced"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// An empty retained payload deletes the retained message, so a removed gateway leaves no state. #[subscriber("fleet/decommissioned")] async fn forget(gone: &Decommissioned, Out(states): Out<impl Publisher, States>) -> HandlerOutcome { let cleared = states .message(&GatewayState(Vec::new())) .to() .gateway(&gone.gateway) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = cleared { tracing::warn!(gone.gateway, %err, "state not cleared"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The state of one gateway, as plain text a dashboard shows as it is. The type carries its own /// bytes, so no codec runs on them, and the `{gateway}` level becomes a setter. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "gateways/{gateway}/state")] struct GatewayState(Vec<u8>); #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(GatewayState)] struct States; /// Turns each heartbeat into the gateway's state. struct Track; impl<Entry> Handle<Heartbeat, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Track where Entry: OutEntry<States, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, heartbeat: &Heartbeat, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let state = if heartbeat.battery_percent < 20 { "low-battery" } else { "ok" }; let announced = outs .get(States) .message(&GatewayState(state.as_bytes().to_vec())) .to() .gateway(&heartbeat.gateway) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = announced { tracing::warn!(heartbeat.gateway, %err, "state not announced"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// An empty retained payload deletes the retained message, so a removed gateway leaves no state. struct Forget; impl<Entry> Handle<Decommissioned, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Forget where Entry: OutEntry<States, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, gone: &Decommissioned, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let cleared = outs .get(States) .message(&GatewayState(Vec::new())) .to() .gateway(&gone.gateway) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = cleared { tracing::warn!(gone.gateway, %err, "state not cleared"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } A state is plain text a dashboard shows as it is, so GatewayState derives Serialized and carries its own bytes, and no codec runs on them. Its topic is a name template: {gateway} becomes a setter, so .to().gateway(..) addresses one gateway's topic. track publishes the state of the gateway each heartbeat comes from. forget publishes an empty payload to the state topic of a gateway that is taken out of service. An empty retained message deletes the retained message of its topic, so the server stops handing that state to new subscribers.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("gateway-monitor", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Runs once the broker is connected, and replaces the will's `offline` of an earlier run. b.after_startup( Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce).retain(true), async move |publisher| -> Result<(), PublishError<MqttError>> { publisher .message(&ServiceStatus(b"online".to_vec())) .publish() .await }, ); // Every state goes out retained, so a dashboard that starts later reads it at once. let retained = Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce).retain(true); b.include(track) .out(States, retained) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("gateways/retry/heartbeat") .build(); b.include(forget).out(States, retained).build(); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "gateway-monitor")) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("gateway-monitor", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Runs once the broker is connected, and replaces the will's `offline` of an earlier run. b.after_startup( Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce).retain(true), async move |publisher| -> Result<(), PublishError<MqttError>> { publisher .message(&ServiceStatus(b"online".to_vec())) .publish() .await }, ); // Every state goes out retained, so a dashboard that starts later reads it at once. let retained = Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce).retain(true); let heartbeats = MqttFilter::new("gateways/+/heartbeat").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce); b.include( subscriber("gateways/+/heartbeat", Track) .map_source(|_| heartbeats) .build(), ) .out(States, retained) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("gateways/retry/heartbeat") .build(); b.include(subscriber("fleet/decommissioned", Forget).build()) .out(States, retained) .build(); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("mqtt://localhost:1883", "gateway-monitor")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } retain(true) on the publish policy makes every publish through the slot retained. Both handlers share the slot States and the policy, so a state and its deletion travel the same way. One message can also be retained on its own: the retain step on a publish overrides the policy for that call. A shared subscription does not receive retained messages when it subscribes. A dashboard that reads the states subscribes outside any share group.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The service's own status, which dashboards read to tell whether it is running. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "services/gateway-monitor/status")] struct ServiceStatus(Vec<u8>); /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `offline` on the /// status topic, retained. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( "services/gateway-monitor/status", "offline", Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } src/main.rs /// The service's own status, which dashboards read to tell whether it is running. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "services/gateway-monitor/status")] struct ServiceStatus(Vec<u8>); /// If the connection ends without a clean disconnect, the server publishes `offline` on the /// status topic, retained. fn broker(url: &str, client_id: &str) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(url, client_id).last_will( "services/gateway-monitor/status", "offline", Qos::AtLeastOnce, true, ) } last_will takes the topic, the payload, the quality of service and the retain flag of the will. The broker hands the will to the server when it connects. If the connection ends without a DISCONNECT packet, because the process crashed or the network failed, the server publishes the will: here offline, retained on services/gateway-monitor/status. A clean shutdown sends DISCONNECT, and the server discards the will. The other half is the after_startup hook in the app above. It runs once the broker is connected and publishes online, retained, to the same topic. So the status topic always holds the latest of the two, and a dashboard that subscribes reads it at once.

The in-process tests check what the service publishes: the state of each gateway, the empty payload of a removed one, and online at startup. The in-process server keeps retained messages as Mosquitto does. The will is published by a server for a connection that ends abruptly, so one test runs against Mosquitto: MQTT_TEST_URL=mqtt://localhost:1883 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 It runs the service, stops it cleanly, and starts a dashboard afterwards: the dashboard receives online and the gateway's state, both retained. Then it ends a run of the service without a DISCONNECT, and the dashboard receives offline. At the end it removes the test's gateway, which clears its state on the server.
This guide installs ruststream-rumqttc, starts a local MQTT server and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-rumqttc = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-rumqttc = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-rumqttc is the MQTT 5 broker. The broker enables no codec of its own, so the service picks json, msgpack or cbor on ruststream. The broker crate has two features, both off by default: Feature What it gives testing the in-process MQTT server behind TestApp asyncapi the MQTT bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document

The rumqttc client speaks TLS through rustls, whose cryptography comes from aws-lc-rs. aws-lc-rs compiles C code, so the build needs a C compiler. On Debian and Ubuntu, build-essential provides it. Other platforms are listed in the aws-lc-rs requirements.

One Eclipse Mosquitto container is enough to develop against. It reads its listeners from a configuration file: mosquitto.conf listener 1883 allow_anonymous true compose.yaml services: mosquitto: image: eclipse-mosquitto:2 ports: - "1883:1883" volumes: - ./mosquitto.conf:/mosquitto/config/mosquitto.conf:ro docker compose up -d The server listens on localhost:1883 and accepts clients without a password.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The coldest temperature a sensor can report; anything below it is a broken sensor. const ABSOLUTE_ZERO: f64 = -273.15; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Telemetry { device: String, temperature: f64, } #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { if telemetry.temperature < ABSOLUTE_ZERO { tracing::warn!(telemetry.device, "impossible reading dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) } src/main.rs /// The coldest temperature a sensor can report; anything below it is a broken sensor. const ABSOLUTE_ZERO: f64 = -273.15; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Telemetry { device: String, temperature: f64, } struct Record; impl Handle<Telemetry> for Record { fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if telemetry.temperature < ABSOLUTE_ZERO { tracing::warn!(telemetry.device, "impossible reading dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "telemetry-svc"), |b| { let fleet = MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce); b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record) .map_source(|_| fleet) .build(), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } record reads the JSON telemetry of every device. It acknowledges a reading and drops one below absolute zero. MqttFilter subscribes to a topic filter: + stands for one level of the topic, here the device's id. Qos::AtLeastOnce makes each reading an acknowledged delivery: the acknowledgement leaves when record returns. A filter matches many topics, so the mount site names the topic a delayed retry goes to; every subscription over a filter names one, and the service refuses to start without it. MqttBroker::new takes the server's URL and the client id, and only records them. The connection opens when the service starts. The client id names the service's session on the server, so each running process has its own. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish a reading from another terminal with the client that ships in the image: docker compose exec mosquitto mosquitto_pub -V mqttv5 -q 1 \ -t devices/dev42/telemetry -m '{"device":"dev42","temperature":21.5}' The service logs reading recorded with the device and its temperature. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes a reading to devices/dev42/telemetry and checks how record settled it. MqttBroker connects to an in-process MQTT server there, so the tests need no Mosquitto: cargo test Testing an MQTT service walks through the tests and what the in-process server models.

A service on rumqttc drives the event loop itself and acknowledges each message by hand. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: rumqttc RustStream MqttOptions and its setters the MqttBroker builder: keep_alive, credentials, clean_start, last_will an EventLoop::poll loop the broker's own connection task, which reconnects and resubscribes AsyncClient::subscribe a #[subscriber] handler on an MqttTopic or an MqttFilter deserializing publish.payload the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec set_manual_acks(true) and AsyncClient::ack the handler's outcome (Delivery guarantees) AsyncClient::publish a reply or an Out parameter, sent through a publish policy (Publishing commands)

A managed MQTT service, such as AWS IoT Core, HiveMQ Cloud or EMQX Cloud, asks for credentials and TLS, often with a client certificate. This guide configures the broker for one, from the deployment's environment.

src/main.rs /// Where the server is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Deployment { url: String, client_id: String, username: String, password: String, ca: Vec<u8>, cert: Vec<u8>, key: Vec<u8>, } impl Deployment { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); let file = |name: &str| fs::read(read(name)).unwrap_or_default(); Self { url: read("MQTT_URL"), client_id: read("MQTT_CLIENT_ID"), username: read("MQTT_USERNAME"), password: read("MQTT_PASSWORD"), ca: file("MQTT_CA"), cert: file("MQTT_CERT"), key: file("MQTT_KEY"), } } } const LARGEST_PACKET: NonZeroU32 = NonZeroU32::new(256 * 1024).unwrap(); const IN_FLIGHT: NonZeroU16 = NonZeroU16::new(200).unwrap(); fn broker(deployment: Deployment) -> MqttBroker { MqttBroker::new(deployment.url, deployment.client_id) .credentials(deployment.username, deployment.password) .tls_ca(deployment.ca) .tls_client_auth(deployment.cert, deployment.key) .keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(30)) .max_packet_size(LARGEST_PACKET) .receive_maximum(IN_FLIGHT) } The deployment provides every setting in environment variables, and the certificates as files. credentials sets the user name and the password of the CONNECT packet. A login inside the URL, such as mqtt://user:p%40ss@host, works too and is percent-decoded; credentials wins over it. They stay out of the generated AsyncAPI document, which reports only the host and port the service connects to. mqtts:// selects TLS, on port 8883 when the URL names none. tls_ca is the certificate authority, in PEM, that the client verifies the server against. The client trusts that authority and no other store, so a mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails the start, naming tls_ca. tls_client_auth adds the client's certificate and key, for a service that authenticates clients by certificate.

The client id is the second argument of MqttBroker::new, and the server keys the session by it. A second connection with the same id takes the session over and closes the first one. So two replicas of a service never share an id: here each takes its own from MQTT_CLIENT_ID, for example the pod's name. Replicas that split the work join a share group instead.

keep_alive is how often the client proves it is alive on an idle connection; the server closes a connection silent for one and a half times as long. The rumqttc client's minimum is 5 seconds, and its default is 60. max_packet_size is the largest packet the service accepts; the server does not send it a larger one. The broker's default is 1 MiB, above the client's own default of 10 KiB. receive_maximum bounds the QoS 1 and 2 deliveries in flight (Delivery guarantees).

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce).shared("ingest"))] async fn record(telemetry: &Telemetry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker(Deployment::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Record; impl Handle<Telemetry> for Record { fn handle( &self, telemetry: &Telemetry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(telemetry.device, telemetry.temperature, "reading recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: MqttBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("telemetry", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let fleet = MqttFilter::new("devices/+/telemetry") .qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) .shared("ingest"); b.include( subscriber("devices/+/telemetry", Record) .map_source(|_| fleet) .build(), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("devices/retry/telemetry"); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker(Deployment::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The broker connects once the service starts. A lost connection reconnects with a backoff that starts at 100 ms and doubles up to 5 seconds, and the broker subscribes again when the server reports the session gone. A refusal the connection will not outgrow ends the connection task instead: bad credentials, a client id the server does not accept, or a TLS handshake the certificates cannot satisfy. Every subscription then returns that error.

The tests start the production service with the production broker, given test settings, under TestApp::start. The in-process server reads the broker's configuration and refuses what the client would refuse, without dialling the server: a keep-alive under 5 seconds fails the start with the client's minimum in the message; a mqtts:// URL without tls_ca fails the start, naming tls_ca. The credentials and the TLS handshake are checked by a real server only. The live tests of the Security page run both against Mosquitto listeners that demand them.

This guide sends commands to one device out of many, at the quality of service each command needs, with headers that a device written in any language reads. The example is a commander service. Operators send a command request to operators/commands. The service forwards each command to the topic of its device, devices/<id>/commands.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// What a device reads on its own command topic; the `{device}` level becomes a setter. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "devices/{device}/commands")] struct DeviceCommand { action: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(DeviceCommand)] struct Commands; src/main.rs /// What a device reads on its own command topic; the `{device}` level becomes a setter. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "devices/{device}/commands")] struct DeviceCommand { action: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(DeviceCommand)] struct Commands; The topic of DeviceCommand is a name template. {device} becomes a setter of the publish, so the handler names the device and the topic follows. Commands is the slot the handler publishes through, and it publishes DeviceCommand only.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Forwards a command to its device. An urgent one goes out at `QoS` 2, every other one at the /// quality of service of the slot's policy; the operator travels as a header. #[subscriber("operators/commands")] async fn dispatch( request: &CommandRequest, Out(commands): Out<impl Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>, Commands>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("operator", request.operator.clone()); let command = DeviceCommand { action: request.action.clone(), }; let message = commands.message(&command).with_headers(headers); let message = if request.urgent { message.qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) } else { message }; if let Err(err) = message.to().device(&request.device).publish().await { tracing::warn!(request.device, %err, "command refused"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(request.device, request.action, "command sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Forwards a command to its device. An urgent one goes out at `QoS` 2, every other one at the /// quality of service of the slot's policy; the operator travels as a header. struct Dispatch; impl<Entry> Handle<CommandRequest, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Dispatch where Entry: OutEntry<Commands, Wire: Publisher<Options = MqttPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, request: &CommandRequest, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("operator", request.operator.clone()); let command = DeviceCommand { action: request.action.clone(), }; let message = outs.get(Commands).message(&command).with_headers(headers); let message = if request.urgent { message.qos(Qos::ExactlyOnce) } else { message }; if let Err(err) = message.to().device(&request.device).publish().await { tracing::warn!(request.device, %err, "command refused"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } tracing::info!(request.device, request.action, "command sent"); Ok(()) } } The slot's policy gives every command its quality of service. An urgent command takes the qos step and goes out at QoS 2 instead. A step changes one message; a setting the call does not name is the policy's. The step writes MqttPublishOptions, so the slot's bound names that type, and the file imports the broker's prelude. retain is the other step, and Device state uses it as a policy. The operator header travels as an MQTT 5 user property. A device reads it as a plain property, with no envelope around the payload. The headers content-type, reply-to and correlation-id take the protocol's own properties instead: the content type, the response topic and the correlation data. publish returns once the client holds the message, before the server confirms it. At QoS 1 and 2 the client sends it again until the server acknowledges it, across reconnects. An error from publish means the client did not take the message: the connection is shut down, or the message breaks the protocol's rules. A topic with + or # breaks them: the request names the device +, the topic becomes devices/+/commands, and dispatch drops the request. A header or a topic with a control character is refused the same way, because a server may close the connection on one.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// States the media type of everything the slot sends, which fills the content type property /// and tells a device to read the body as UTF-8 text. struct Json; impl<K: ContextKind, Options> PublishTransform<K, Options> for Json { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &K::View<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("content-type", "application/json"); } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("commander", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "commander"), |b| { b.include(dispatch) .out(Commands, Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce)) .transform(Json) .build(); }, ) } src/main.rs /// States the media type of everything the slot sends, which fills the content type property /// and tells a device to read the body as UTF-8 text. struct Json; impl<K: ContextKind, Options> PublishTransform<K, Options> for Json { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &K::View<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("content-type", "application/json"); } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("commander", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "commander"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("operators/commands", Dispatch).build()) .out(Commands, Publish::default().qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce)) .transform(Json) .build(); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The mount site gives the slot its policy, QoS 1, and a publish transform. Json puts content-type: application/json on every command the slot sends. The broker turns it into the content type property and sets the payload format indicator, so a device reads the body as UTF-8 text. The codec does not write the header itself: a transform at the mount site is where a service states its media type once.

The tests in the example file run the app in process and read the commands the slot published. tb.out::<Commands>() shows the per-message settings: none for a routine command, QoS 2 for an urgent one. published on devices/dev42/commands shows the payload and both headers. The in-process server validates topics and headers the way the client does, so the request for device + is dropped there too.

This guide answers MQTT 5 requests: each answer goes to the topic its request names and carries the request's correlation data. MQTT 5 gives a request two properties for this. The response topic says where the answer goes. The correlation data is an opaque value the requester uses to match an answer to its question. The broker maps them onto the reply-to and correlation-id headers in both directions. The example is a device agent. Consoles ask it for one setting on devices/dev42/config/get, and it answers with the setting's value.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Asks the device for one setting. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "devices/dev42/config/get")] struct ConfigQuery { key: String, } /// The answer. The type names no topic: each query says where its answer goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct ConfigValue { key: String, value: String, } /// Stands in for the device's settings. fn setting(key: &str) -> Option<&'static str> { match key { "sample-interval" => Some("30s"), "firmware" => Some("2.1.0"), _ => None, } } /// A query without a response topic is answered on the topic the mount site names; a key the /// device does not have gets no answer. #[subscriber( MqttTopic::new("devices/dev42/config/get"), reply("devices/dev42/config") )] async fn answer(query: &ConfigQuery) -> Result<ConfigValue, HandlerOutcome> { let Some(value) = setting(&query.key) else { tracing::warn!(query.key, "unknown setting"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; tracing::info!(query.key, "setting reported"); Ok(ConfigValue { key: query.key.clone(), value: value.to_owned(), }) } src/main.rs /// Asks the device for one setting. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "devices/dev42/config/get")] struct ConfigQuery { key: String, } /// The answer. The type names no topic: each query says where its answer goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ConfigValue { key: String, value: String, } /// Stands in for the device's settings. fn setting(key: &str) -> Option<&'static str> { match key { "sample-interval" => Some("30s"), "firmware" => Some("2.1.0"), _ => None, } } /// A key the device does not have gets no answer. struct Answer; impl Handle<ConfigQuery, ConfigValue> for Answer { fn handle( &self, query: &ConfigQuery, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<ConfigValue, HandlerOutcome>> { let Some(value) = setting(&query.key) else { tracing::warn!(query.key, "unknown setting"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); }; tracing::info!(query.key, "setting reported"); ready(Ok(ConfigValue { key: query.key.clone(), value: value.to_owned(), })) } } A responder is an ordinary handler with a reply: the value it returns is published. ConfigValue names no topic, so the mount site names one: reply("devices/dev42/config"). That topic is the fallback, for a request that carries no response topic. A setting the device does not have ends in drop, and nothing is published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Sends the answer to the response topic of the query, which arrives as the `reply-to` header, /// and copies the query's correlation data, so the requester matches the answer to its question. struct ToResponseTopic; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToResponseTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(topic) = cx.headers().reply_to() { out.set_name(topic.to_owned()); } if let Some(id) = cx.headers().correlation_id() { out.headers_mut().insert("correlation-id", id.to_owned()); } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("device-agent", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "device-agent-dev42"), |b| { b.include(answer) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ToResponseTopic); }, ) } src/main.rs /// Sends the answer to the response topic of the query, which arrives as the `reply-to` header, /// and copies the query's correlation data, so the requester matches the answer to its question. struct ToResponseTopic; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToResponseTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(topic) = cx.headers().reply_to() { out.set_name(topic.to_owned()); } if let Some(id) = cx.headers().correlation_id() { out.headers_mut().insert("correlation-id", id.to_owned()); } } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("device-agent", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "device-agent-dev42"), |b| { // A query without a response topic is answered on the topic named here. let answer = subscriber("devices/dev42/config/get", Answer) .reply() .to("devices/dev42/config") .build(); b.include(answer) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ToResponseTopic); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } ToResponseTopic is a publish transform on the reply position. It reads the request's headers: reply-to becomes the answer's topic, and correlation-id is copied onto the answer. It declares Destination = Names, which gives it the right to choose the topic. A request without reply-to keeps the mount site's topic. The AsyncAPI document of the service reports the reply's address as the request's reply-to header, $message.header#/reply-to, because no fixed channel holds the answers.

The requester is any MQTT 5 client. Mosquitto ships one, mosquitto_rr, which publishes a request with a response topic and prints the answer: docker compose exec mosquitto mosquitto_rr \ -t devices/dev42/config/get -e consoles/c1/responses -m '{"key":"firmware"}' It prints {"key":"firmware","value":"2.1.0"}. A requester inside a RustStream service publishes the request with both headers set, and reads the answers with a subscriber on its own response topic.

The tests in the example file publish a query with reply-to and correlation-id headers, in process. The headers reach the handler through the same mapping onto MQTT 5 properties as on the wire. The tests check the answer on consoles/c1/responses with its correlation data, the fallback topic for a query without a response topic, and that an unknown setting gets no answer.

This guide retries a message now or later, caps the attempts and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter topic. MQTT holds no message back, counts no deliveries and has no dead-letter queue. The framework does all three: the mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter topic, and a retry travels as a copy of the message with a retry count in a header. The example is a firmware service. It installs updates on devices, and a device may refuse an update for a while. It also stores the reports every device sends.

A device refuses an update in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means it is running a job: an update offered now is refused again, so retry_after offers it in 30 seconds. Interrupted means the transfer broke off: retry tries again at once. Incompatible means the image does not fit the device, and another try gets the same answer, so the update is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("updates/install").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn install(update: &Update) -> HandlerOutcome { match flash(update).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(Refusal::Busy) => { tracing::info!(update.device, "device busy, offering the update later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF) } Err(Refusal::Interrupted) => { tracing::warn!(update.device, "transfer interrupted, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } Err(Refusal::Incompatible) => { tracing::warn!(update.device, update.version, "incompatible image dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs struct Install; impl Handle<Update> for Install { async fn handle( &self, update: &Update, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match flash(update).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(Refusal::Busy) => { tracing::info!(update.device, "device busy, offering the update later"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)) } Err(Refusal::Interrupted) => { tracing::warn!(update.device, "transfer interrupted, retrying"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } Err(Refusal::Incompatible) => { tracing::warn!(update.device, update.version, "incompatible image dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } fn updates() -> MqttTopic { MqttTopic::new("updates/install").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) } retry_after acknowledges the delivery, waits, then publishes a copy back to updates/install. The copy carries the retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. It works at every quality of service; a QoS 0 delivery has nothing to acknowledge, and its copy is published all the same. The copy waits in the service's memory: a process that stops before the delay ends loses it. retry becomes a copy too, published at once, because the mount site below declares a cap. MQTT counts no redeliveries, so the cap counts the copies through their header. Without a cap, retry leaves the delivery unacknowledged for the next session, as Delivery guarantees shows.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("firmware", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc"), |b| { // Four deliveries of one update, the first included; the fourth refusal moves it to // "updates/dead", payload and headers as they arrived. b.include(install) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("updates/dead"); b.include(review); b.include(record) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("reports/dead") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToDeliveryTopic); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("firmware", "0.1.0")).with_broker( MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "firmware-svc"), |b| { // Four deliveries of one update, the first included; the fourth refusal moves it to // "updates/dead", payload and headers as they arrived. b.include( subscriber("updates/install", Install) .map_source(|_| updates()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("updates/dead"); b.include( subscriber("updates/dead", Review) .map_source(|_| dead_updates()) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber("devices/+/reports", Record) .map_source(|_| reports()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("reports/dead") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToDeliveryTopic); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one update, the first included. The fourth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to updates/dead, payload and headers as they arrived. A dropped update settles and goes nowhere; the dead-letter topic holds only the updates that ran out of attempts. A copy is an ordinary publish, so every subscription whose filter matches its topic receives it, in this service and in any other. So each retried topic and each dead-letter topic lies outside every other filter the service reads. An updates/# subscription next to install would read every copy of every update, and every dead letter too.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The dead-letter topic is read like any other; the retry-count header says how many times the /// update was delivered before it was moved there. #[subscriber(MqttTopic::new("updates/dead").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn review(update: &Update, ctx: &mut Context) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!( update.device, update.version, deliveries, "update needs a person" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The dead-letter topic is read like any other; the retry-count header says how many times the /// update was delivered before it was moved there. struct Review; impl Handle<Update> for Review { fn handle( &self, update: &Update, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!( update.device, update.version, deliveries, "update needs a person" ); ready(Ok(())) } } fn dead_updates() -> MqttTopic { MqttTopic::new("updates/dead").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) } The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and review reads it like any other. The retry-count header of a dead-lettered update holds the number of deliveries it went through, 4 here.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Sends every copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on, the one topic of the filter's many /// that the report belongs to. struct ToDeliveryTopic; impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<MqttContext>, Options> for ToDeliveryTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, MqttContext>, ) { out.set_name(cx.context(DeliveryTopic).to_owned()); } } /// The `Ctx<DeliveryTopic>` parameter makes the crate's context the registration's, which is /// what the transform reads. #[subscriber(MqttFilter::new("devices/+/reports").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce))] async fn record(report: &Report, Ctx(topic): Ctx<DeliveryTopic>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = store(report).await { tracing::warn!(%topic, %err, "report not stored, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Sends every copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on, the one topic of the filter's many /// that the report belongs to. struct ToDeliveryTopic; impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<MqttContext>, Options> for ToDeliveryTopic { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, MqttContext>, ) { out.set_name(cx.context(DeliveryTopic).to_owned()); } } /// A body typed over `MqttContext` makes the crate's context the registration's, which is what /// the transform reads. struct Record; impl Handle<Report, (), (), MqttContext> for Record { async fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MqttContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if let Err(err) = store(report).await { let topic = ctx.context(DeliveryTopic); tracing::warn!(%topic, %err, "report not stored, retrying"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)); } Ok(()) } } fn reports() -> MqttFilter { MqttFilter::new("devices/+/reports").qos(Qos::AtLeastOnce) } A copy of a delivery on an MqttTopic goes back to that topic. An MqttFilter matches many topics and names none, so its registration names where a copy goes, and the service refuses to start without it. out_retry(Publish::default()).to(..) names one topic for every copy. ToDeliveryTopic names one per delivery instead: it reads the topic the report arrived on from the MQTT context and sends the copy back there. So a report from devices/dev7/reports comes back on devices/dev7/reports, to record alone. The handler takes Ctx<DeliveryTopic>, which gives the registration the MQTT context; in the manual form its context type is MqttContext.

The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. They count the deliveries of each update, read the retry-count header of each copy, and check what reaches updates/dead. Testing an MQTT service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process MQTT server or against Mosquitto. The service under test watches freezers. Each freezer publishes its temperature to freezers/<id>/temperature, and the monitors share the readings in a share group. Every reading goes into a temperature log. A freezer warmer than -18 °C raises an alert on freezers/alerts. When the log does not answer, the handler asks for the reading again in ten seconds with retry_after. After three deliveries a reading goes to freezers/review, the dead-letter topic. The handler watch publishes the alert through an Alerts slot. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-rumqttc in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_warm_freezer_raises_an_alert() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let broker = MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "cold-chain"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert(tb).await } async fn a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert( tb: TestApp<()>, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .message(&reading("f1", -12.5)) .to("freezers/f1/temperature") .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .subscriber("freezers/+/temperature") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .published::<Alert>("freezers/alerts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Alert { freezer: "f1".to_owned(), celsius: -12.5, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_warm_freezer_raises_an_alert() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let broker = MqttBroker::new("mqtt://localhost:1883", "cold-chain"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert(tb).await } async fn a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert( tb: TestApp<()>, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .message(&reading("f1", -12.5)) .to("freezers/f1/temperature") .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .subscriber("freezers/+/temperature") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<MqttBroker>() .published::<Alert>("freezers/alerts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Alert { freezer: "f1".to_owned(), celsius: -12.5, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects MqttBroker to an in-process MQTT server. A Reading names no topic, so the test names one with .to("freezers/f1/temperature"), as a freezer would. The handler's filter matches it the way Mosquitto would. publish returns once the handler and its alert have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscription settled and what reached freezers/alerts. The subscription is addressed by its filter, without the share group. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

documents.t: The in-process server reads the broker's own settings, and a publish goes through the same validation and the same mapping onto MQTT 5 properties as on the wire. It models the server one connection talks to: A publish reaches every subscription whose filter matches its topic, with +, # and the rule for topics that start with $. A share group takes one copy between its members, and overlapping filters each receive their own. A retained message reaches a later subscription outside a share group, and an empty retained payload clears it. A message larger than max_packet_size never arrives, and a topic or header the client refuses fails the publish. An acknowledgement after shutdown is refused. Each broker connected in process is a server of its own. A persistent session and its resumption, the last will, the receive-maximum window, the QoS 1 and 2 handshakes and several connections on one server need a real broker.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_warm_freezer_raises_an_alert_on_mosquitto() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let Some(url) = live::url("MQTT_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let broker = MqttBroker::new(url, live::client_id("cold-chain")); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert(tb).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_warm_freezer_raises_an_alert_on_mosquitto() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let Some(url) = live::url("MQTT_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let broker = MqttBroker::new(url, live::client_id("cold-chain")); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_warm_reading_raises_one_alert(tb).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running server. The test reads the address from MQTT_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and returns at once when it is unset. It connects with a client id of its own, so it shares the server with other runs.
